qs.q: Which genetic alterations are strongly associated with small-cell carcinoma of the bladder?
o: Loss‑of‑function mutations in TP53 and RB
qs.e: Small-cell carcinoma of the bladder is strongly associated with loss-of-function mutations in the TP53 and RB tumour suppressor genes. It is histologically indistinguishable from small-cell lung cancer.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man with a history of bladder cancer presents with a new mass. Biopsy shows a tumour that is histologically identical to small-cell carcinoma of the lung. Which underlying genetic defect is most characteristic of this tumour?
qs.e: Small-cell carcinoma of the bladder is strongly associated with loss-of-function mutations in TP53 and RB. FGFR3 mutations are more common in low-grade urothelial cancers.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with small cell carcinoma of the lung develops progressive proximal muscle weakness and diminished deep tendon reflexes that improve with sustained muscle contraction. Laboratory investigation confirms autoantibodies directed against presynaptic calcium channels. What is this paraneoplastic neurological syndrome called?
qs.e: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a paraneoplastic manifestation of small cell lung cancer caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels. Cushing's syndrome is caused by ectopic ACTH, and hypercalcaemia by PTHrP.
qs.s: Essential Cardiovascular Pathology: Atherosclerosis to Endoc: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with suspected small cell lung carcinoma undergoes a diagnostic biopsy. Beyond standard morphology, which immunohistochemical markers are classically associated with neuroendocrine tumors like small cell carcinoma?
o: CD45, CD20, and CD3 lymphocyte markers
qs.e: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD56 are hallmark immunohistochemical markers for neuroendocrine tumors. CD45, CD20, and CD3 are instead utilized for identifying lymphomas.
qs.s: Pathology Practical and Stains Revision Guide: MCQs

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Small cell carcinoma is an aggressive, central lung cancer of neuroendocrine origin, strongly linked to smoking and paraneoplastic syndromes. Diagnosis relies on morphology and neuroendocrine markers; staging determines prognosis and therapy.

sections.p: A high‑grade neuroendocrine carcinoma arising in the central bronchi, composed of small round cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, and high mitotic rate. Diagnosis requires histology plus immunostains (chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56).
b: Requires tissue biopsy; cytology from bronchial washings may suffice in resource‑limited settings

t.b: Confirms a central mass and assesses local invasion; a mass >3 cm suggests advanced disease
Provides tissue for histology and immunostaining; definitive diagnosis

sections.p: Staged with the limited vs extensive system (TNM can also be used). Limited disease is confined to one hemithorax and regional nodes; extensive disease spreads beyond.
b: Limited disease may be curable with chemoradiation; extensive disease requires systemic therapy

sections.p: Strongly associated with tobacco exposure; other risk factors include prior lung disease and possibly genetic susceptibility. No infectious cause, but HIV patients smoke more and may present earlier.
b: Smoking is the dominant cause; cessation reduces risk

sections.p: Patients often have cough, dyspnea, weight loss, and may develop paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH, Cushing’s, or Lambert‑Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
b: Rapid symptom progression over weeks; look for hyponatremia or ectopic ACTH signs

sections.p: A combination of imaging, pathology, and labs identifies disease extent and paraneoplastic effects.

t.b: Detects SIADH; low sodium (<135 mmol/L) suggests ectopic ADH
Screens for ectopic ACTH production; elevated cortisol with lack of suppression
Identify Lambert‑Eaton; decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation

sections.p: Rapid respiratory decline, massive hemoptysis, paraneoplastic crises (severe hyponatremia, hypercortisolism), and brain metastases can be life‑threatening.
b: Urgent care needed for severe hyponatremia <120 mmol/L or neurologic deterioration

sections.p: First treat the tumor with systemic chemotherapy (platinum‑etoposide) and consider radiotherapy for limited disease. Manage paraneoplastic syndromes supportively.
b: Platinum‑based chemo targets rapidly dividing cells; avoids agents causing excessive myelosuppression in fragile patients

sections.p: Regular imaging every 2–3 months to detect recurrence; monitor electrolytes for paraneoplastic relapse. Primary prevention is smoking cessation and early detection of lung lesions.
b: Low‑dose CT screening in high‑risk smokers reduces late‑stage presentation

sections.p: Other central lung cancers and metastatic neuroendocrine tumors can mimic small cell carcinoma histologically.
Neuroendocrine markers may be weakly positive in non‑small cell cancers; normal sodium does not exclude SIADH early on.
b: Interpret labs in clinical context; repeat tests if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hyponatremia causing seizures, sudden worsening dyspnea, massive hemoptysis, new neurologic deficits

faq.q: Why is small cell carcinoma considered a neuroendocrine tumor?
faq.a: The cells express neuroendocrine markers and can secrete hormones like ADH or ACTH, causing paraneoplastic syndromes.

faq.q: What distinguishes limited from extensive disease?
faq.a: Limited disease is confined to one hemithorax and regional nodes; extensive disease has spread beyond, influencing treatment choice.

faq.q: Can small cell carcinoma arise outside the lung?
faq.a: Yes, extrapulmonary small cell carcinoma exists but is rare; diagnosis follows the same neuroendocrine criteria.
